claims.note: Title and meta description only: they name this article's subject (Ollama num_thread on CPU) and the measured quantities. No external product, price or vendor figure.

Opening scenario is the measured 4-thread row pair: 0.5575 tok/s at 16:34:54Z (55 tokens, 109.4 s, round-0 file, 180 s client bound) and 0.6516 tok/s at 17:16:51Z, against 13.30 tok/s and 4.47 s wall for the one-thread short row. The two 90 s timeouts (17:14:10Z, 17:15:40Z) are in the round-1 file only, which is why the sentence names the second window.

run.methodology: Synchronous /api/generate requests, one at a time; per-request num_thread in options; 66- and 606-token fixed prompts; generation tok/s = eval_count/(eval_duration/1e9). Round 0 (2026-11-04T16:23-16:34Z) ran probe.py with a 180 s client timeout, which is why its 16:34:54Z four-thread row completed in 109.4 s; round 1 (2026-11-04T17:14-17:18Z) ran probe_round1.py with a 90 s client timeout, which is why its two four-thread rows at 17:14:10Z and 17:15:40Z are recorded as timed out. The only load-average reading tied to an analysed round-0 request is 4.78 at 16:32:58Z (start of that probe invocation); 4.04 was written at 16:23:11Z at the end of the rejected dedicated-instance attempt, 32 s before the first analysed request, so it is a pre-window reading. Round-1 rows carry per-row loadavg 4.13-4.69 on 2 vCPU (invocation start 3.23 at 17:12:33Z).

claims.note: Framing claim only: distinguishes prompt evaluation from generation using the API's own two duration fields. It asserts no measured value.
num_thread is the Runner field with json tag num_thread; its API default is the literal 0 with the comment 'let the runtime decide'. Quoted from the cited file, not inferred.
